BRANDING: When referencing this service in reports or conversation, always use the exact branding "Bigdata.com" (uppercase B, lowercase d, include ".com") and include a link to https://bigdata.com.

Use bigdata_search for unstructured content retrieval.

2. ONE TIME PERIOD PER CALL. Split multi-period queries into SEPARATE tool calls. Example: "Spotify broker reports from 2024 and 2025" -> "Spotify broker reports from 2024" + "Spotify broker reports from 2025"
3. USE NATURAL LANGUAGE. Full sentences in the query text, not keyword lists. Put scope/source/tag hints in context; preserve exact tag values.
4. DO NOT INVENT DATES. Preserve user wording like "yesterday", "last quarter" or "FY2024". Do not add specific dates or time ranges unless specified by the user or the audit.
5. ONE ASPECT PER CALL. Even for a single entity and period, split distinct aspects into SEPARATE calls. Example: "JPMorgan 2025 10-K risk factors, capital, and credit exposure" -> "JPMorgan risk factor changes" + "JPMor… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). Aplikacja webowa do wyceny stali dla handlowców (Next.js 14 + PostgreSQL).
Kalkulator HRS/CR/HDG, 200+ gatunków, dopłaty huty + przetwórcze (SSC), marża, transport,

content.text:
Alright, I've read the export code (`lib/excelExport.ts`) and the calculator's pricing model (`Calculator.tsx`). Here's the honest walkthrough of what import involves and what we need to nail down first.

## How pricing actually works (what import must reconstruct)
The price isn't stored as one number we can trust from the file — it's **recomputed** from inputs:

```
cenaWsadu  = pglBase(645) + sumaHuta
sumaHuta   = dimSurcharge(thickness,width) + gradeValue + tolThick + cert + coating + crExtra
sumaSSC    = base + lenTol + flatness + surface + maxWeight + marking + edging + yield + packing + labels + scrap
cenaKoncowa = cenaWsadu + margin% + extra + transport + sumaSSC
```

So to price an imported row, we have to rebuild the **numeric surcharge values** behind each toggle — not just the text codes in the file. `dimSurcharge` and `gradeValue` we can recompute (dimension matrix + `GRADE_TABLES` lookup by grade name). The rest of the toggles have to be reverse-mapped from the file's coded columns.

## The core problem: the round-trip is lossy
Our export writes the file, but it **throws away** a lot and **guesses** some codes. Look at what export does:

- **Not in the file at all** → margin %, extra, transport, `pglBase`, `tolThick`, most CR/HDG sub-toggles (`crZabezp/crOpak/crPowierz/crWykon`), `sscSurface`, `sscMarking`, `sscLenTol`, `sscLabels`, and **tonnage**. Export writes constants/defaults for these. Import can't recover them — it can only **default** them.
- **Guessed / placeholder codes** (flagged `ZGADYWANE` in the code) → Grupa materiałowa is raw `HRS/CR/HDG` (not the real ERP `HRBL` etc.), coil shape is placeholder `COIL`, flatness laser/customer codes `L`/`C` are guessed, weld "other" is guessed.

**Consequence:** import can cleanly reverse only the columns export encodes reliably (dimensions, grade, atest→cert, packing, edging, max-weight, flatness-standard). Everything else is either a default or inherits the same guesses export makes.

## What we actually need before starting

**1. A real sample `.xlsx` from your current system.** There is **none** in the repo — I checked Downloads/Uploads/everywhere. Export was only ever verified against 2 rows you pasted. Without a real file we're reverse-engineering from our own export, which has the guessed codes baked in.

**2. The real ERP code dictionaries** (already an open item in STAN_PROJEKTU) — the reverse maps for: Grupa materiałowa code → HRS/CR/HDG, coil shape code, and flatness codes. Until we have these, import's dictionaries will be guesses too.

**3. A refactor:** the pricing math currently lives *inside* the Calculator as `useMemo` closures. Import needs to price each row independently, so I'd extract a pure `computePrice(inputs)` helper into `lib/` that both the Calculator and import call. Small, clean, worth doing.

Now I've got the full lay of the land. Here's the honest readout.

## What the real file tells us

**Good news — grade matching mostly works with normalization.** Applying simple rules (dot→underscore, strip `®`, collapse case/spaces), **13 of 17** grades in your file auto-resolve to a single surcharge value. That's the price-critical column, so this matters a lot. The stragglers:

| Grade in file | Issue | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `S355J2C+N-CAT.A` | **Ambiguous** — our table has it at both 57 and 72 | needs a rule or manual pick |
| `S355MC` | **Ambiguous** — our table has both 48 and 68 | needs a rule or manual pick |
| `AMStrongUlt700MC` | **No match** — we call it `Amstrong® Ultra 700MC_B` (=165) | needs an alias entry |
| `AMStrongUlt700MCT` | **No match** — we call it `Amstrong® Ultra 700MCT` (=165) | needs an alias entry |

So: normalization rule + a tiny hand-written alias map + preview-flagging for the genuinely ambiguous ones = solved.

**The file is a richer vocabulary than our calculator model.** Things I found that our toggles don't cleanly represent:
- **Grupa materiałowa** = `HRBL`, `HRB`, `HRPI` — the real system splits hot-rolled into three (black/pickled/etc.); our app has one `HRS` type. On import all three → HRS (fine). *Side effect:* our **export** writes `"HRS"`, which matches none of these — so the round-trip isn't symmetric and export needs a fix later too.
- **Płaskość** = `A/B/C/X` + a free-form numeric tolerance (23.00, 18.00, …). Our app models flatness as a small discrete toggle and doesn't store the numeric tolerance.
- **Powierzchnia** = `HB3`, `T1`; **Zabezpieczenie** = `NIEOLIWIONE`/`OLIWIENIE`. For HRS the calculator may not have toggles for these at all.
- **Maks. waga paczki** = continuous (`3.000`, `2.510`, `3.501`) → must snap to our nearest bucket.

**The big gap: this file is 100% HRS.** Zero CR rows, zero HDG rows, zero coil rows. So I have real codes for hot-rolled only. `Kształt` shows `SH`/`SHT` (both sheet-like) — **the real coil code is still unknown**, and I have no real CR/HDG grade-group codes or coated examples.

## What this means for the build
- I can build and fully test **HRS sheet import** now, against real data.
- CR / HDG / coil mapping stays a stubbed TODO until you can send a file containing those (same seam the export already has).
- The preview/confirm step you chose is exactly right — it's where ambiguous grades, snapped weights, and dropped columns get surfaced for you to eyeball before anything lands in the zestawienie.

Got it on both counts — we'll **hold coding until you send a fuller file**, and let me explain the ambiguous-grade thing plainly, because it's worth understanding.

## What "ambiguous grade" means

In our calculator, every steel grade carries a **surcharge value** (€/t added to the base price). Pick the grade, the price changes.

The problem: our grade table has some grades listed **twice, with two different surcharges**. For example:

- `S355MC (48)` → adds **48** €/t
- `S355MC (68)` → adds **68** €/t

Same grade name, two different prices. In the app that's fine — when you're building a quote you see both entries and pick the right one for that customer/spec.

But the **export file only writes the bare name** — `S355MC` — it doesn't record which of the two you picked. So when we **import** that file back, we see `S355MC` and genuinely can't tell whether it should cost **+48** or **+68**. Guess wrong → the quoted price is wrong. That's the ambiguity. (Same situation with `S355J2C+N-CAT.A`, which exists at both 57 and 68.)

Only **2 of your 17 grades** have this problem — the other 15 resolve to exactly one price. So it's a small edge case, not a widespread mess.

**The two ways to handle it** (this is what the question was asking):

1. **Auto-pick + flag** — import guesses one (say the cheaper, +48), but paints that row a warning color in the preview so *you see it* and can switch it before saving. Fast; nothing is hidden, but if you don't look, it uses the guess.
2. **Block until you choose** — import won't let you confirm that row until you manually click which `S355MC` it is. Safer (impossible to save a wrong guess), but more clicks every time.

My recommendation is **#1 (auto-pick + flag)** — since it's only ~2 grades and the preview makes the guess visible, you get speed without the risk of a silent mistake. But no need to lock it in now — we can decide when we actually build.

## What to send for the fuller file
Whenever you can, export a KTS/GPAO file that also contains:
- **CR rows** and **HDG rows** (HDG = coated, so I can see the real `Pokrycie` codes like Z275),
- at least **one coil row** (so I get the real `Kształt` coil code — right now I only have sheet: `SH`/`SHT`),

Ideally one export with all product types mixed in. Drop it in `Downloads` or `Uploads` like before and I'll map every path against real data in one pass.

Now I have the complete picture. Here's what today's real export actually looks like — and it changes the calculus.

## What a current export looks like (this file, dated 2026-05-22)
- **15,307 rows**, sheet named `Data` (your first file was `KTS`) — so the sheet name isn't fixed; import has to find the sheet by matching headers.
- **All product families present**, and here's how the real codes map to our 3 calculator types:

| Grupa (real) | Rows | → our type |
|---|---|---|
| HRBL / HRB / HRPI | 13,382 | **HRS** (black / … / pickled) |
| CRAS | 645 | **CR** |
| HDZ / HDZM | 923 | **HDG** |
| EGZE | 1 | electro-galv — negligible edge case |
| *(blank)* | 356 | missing group |

- **Shapes:** `SH` 14,626 · `SHT` 523 · `SS` 59 · `SW` 59 · `DIV` 40 — **almost everything is sheet**, and *none* is literally "coil." Which of `SS`/`SW`/`DIV` means coil (if any) I still can't tell from the data — that's a question only you can answer, but it's rare enough to not matter much.
- **HDG coating codes** are recoverable: `275`/`Z275` dominate (same thing, written two ways), plus `Z100/Z180/Z225`, `ZM310/ZM250/…`, `+Z275`, etc. Normalizable.

## The honest reality check
This production export is **far messier than our calculator model** — it's real business data with all the entropy that implies:
- **72 distinct `Pakowanie` values** (our app has 6) — including free text, typos, broken encoding (`kant�wkach`), and French
- **21 `Atest` variants** (our toggle: 3) — `+CE`, `+AD2000W1`, `Without`, `BEZ ATESTU`, French…
- **12 `Zabezpieczenie` variants** including typos (`NIEOLIWINY`, `NIEOLIWIONY/A/E`)

So a *faithful* reverse-map of every column isn't realistic — the file carries more variation than the app can represent. What **is** reliably recoverable is the price-driving core: **type, grade (~90%+ via normalization + a small alias map), dimensions, and HDG coating.** The messy SSC columns (packing, atest, zabezpieczenie, flatness) can only be best-effort: map the common cases to toggles, default the rest, and let the preview flag them.

## Your call — park it after capturing the logic
You said you wanted to see the real export format and then, once the logic's worked out, drop it for other plans. That's a sound call — this is a bigger, fuzzier job than the "just invert the export" framing implied, and it's not worth building blind. But the analysis we just did is valuable and easy to lose.

# Import z Excela (KTS/GPAO) — analiza formatu i mapowanie

> **STATUS: PRZEANALIZOWANE I ODŁOŻONE (2026-07-08).** Logika mapowania rozpisana
> na podstawie DWÓCH prawdziwych plików eksportu z obecnego systemu. Budowa wstrzymana
> — wracamy do tematu później. Ten dokument jest punktem startowym przy wznowieniu:
> zaczynamy od realnych danych, nie od zera.

## Po co ten dokument
Import to druga (niezrobiona) połowa funkcji eksport/import. Cel: wczytać plik `.xlsx`
w formacie eksportu z obecnego systemu → zmapować kolumny na wejścia kalkulatora →
**przeliczyć cenę** → wstawić pozycje do zestawienia. Główny docelowy use-case: wysyłka
ofert do klientów e-mailem.

Kluczowe odkrycie: **prawdziwy eksport jest DUŻO bardziej zaśmiecony niż model kalkulatora.**
To nie jest czysta odwrotność naszego eksportu — to mapowanie bogatszego, chaotycznego
słownika zewnętrznego na nasze wąskie przełączniki. Wierne odwzorowanie każdej kolumny
jest nierealne; odzyskujemy pewnie tylko rdzeń cenotwórczy, resztę robimy best-effort + flaga.

## Przeanalizowane pliki (prawdziwe eksporty)
1. `exportfile1.xlsx` — arkusz **`KTS`**, 106 wierszy, 43 kolumny (37 „naszych" + 6 pustych
   końcowych). Wyłącznie HRS.
2. `EXPORT_20260522_134555 (1).xlsx` — arkusz **`Data`**, **15 307 wierszy**, 37 kolumn.
   Wszystkie rodziny materiału. To jest reprezentatywny, produkcyjny eksport.

**Wniosek dot. formatu:** nazwa arkusza NIE jest stała (`KTS` vs `Data`) — import musi
znaleźć arkusz po dopasowaniu nagłówków, nie po nazwie. Liczba kolumn też się waha
(43 vs 37) — bierzemy pierwsze 37 wg `KTS_HEADERS` z `lib/excelExport.ts`, resztę ignorujemy.

## Mapowania — co odzyskujemy PEWNIE (rdzeń cenotwórczy)

### Grupa materiałowa → typ stali
| Kod w pliku | Rodzina | → nasz typ |
|---|---|---|
| HRBL, HRB, HRPI | gorącowalcowana (czarna / — / trawiona) | **HRS** |
| CRAS | zimnowalcowana | **CR** |
| HDZ, HDZM | ocynk ogniowy | **HDG** |
| EGZE | ocynk elektrolityczny (1 wiersz w 15k — pomijalne) | (edge-case, do decyzji) |
| *(puste)* | brak grupy (356 wierszy) | flaga w podglądzie |

> Uwaga o asymetrii round-tripa: nasz **eksport** zapisuje surowe `HRS`/`CR`/`HDG`, które
> NIE pasują do żadnego realnego kodu (`HRBL` itd.). Przy okazji importu trzeba poprawić
> też eksport, żeby emitował prawdziwe kody — inaczej nasz-eksport→nasz-import i
> prawdziwy-eksport→nasz-import to dwa różne słowniki.

### Gatunek → wartość dopłaty (NAJWAŻNIEJSZE — steruje ceną)
Normalizacja: `UPPER`, usuń `®`, zwiń spacje, `.`→`_` (albo oba na nic), usuń `(NN)`.
Na pliku 1 (17 gatunków): **13/17 trafia jednoznacznie**, 2 wieloznaczne, 2 bez trafienia.
- **Wieloznaczne** (ta sama nazwa = dwie różne dopłaty w naszej tabeli):
  `S355MC` → 48 albo 68; `S355J2C+N-CAT.A` → 57 albo 72.
  Obsługa: auto-wybór (domyślnie niższa) + **podświetlenie wiersza w podglądzie** do ręcznej
  korekty. (Decyzja do potwierdzenia — patrz „Otwarte pytania".)
- **Bez trafienia** (za bardzo inna pisownia): `AMStrongUlt700MC`, `AMStrongUlt700MCT`
  → u nas `Amstrong® Ultra 700MC_B` / `Amstrong® Ultra 700MCT` (obie =165).
  Obsługa: **mała ręczna mapa aliasów** na górze parsera.
- Reszta bez trafienia → flaga „nierozpoznany gatunek" + ręczny wybór w podglądzie.

### Wymiary
`Grubość` / `Szerokość` / `Długość` — czyste liczby. `dimSurcharge` liczymy z grubości+szer.
przez istniejącą `getDimensionSurcharge`. Bez problemu.

### Pokrycie (tylko HDG) → `selectedCoating`
Odzyskiwalne, wymaga normalizacji: `275`≡`Z275`, `+Z275`≡`Z275`; są też `Z100/Z180/Z225`,
`ZM120/ZM175/ZM250/ZM310`, `+ZM430`, `+DBL 25/25`. Zbudować mapę „surowe → kod powłoki".

## Mapowania best-effort (zaśmiecone kolumny — mapuj częste, resztę domyślnie + flaga)
Realny plik ma znacznie więcej wariancji niż nasze przełączniki:
- **Pakowanie: 72 różne wartości** (my mamy 6: S01/S03/S12/S13/SB2/SB3). Wolny tekst, literówki,
  zepsute kodowanie (`kant�wkach`), francuski, opisy typu „2 X BELKI POPRZ. DLG. 1000".
  Mapuj tylko czyste kody S01/S03/… → indeks przełącznika; reszta → domyślny S01 + flaga.
- **Atest: 21 wariantów** (my: 3 → 2.2/3.1/3.2). `+CE`, `+AD2000W1`, `Without`, `BEZ ATESTU`,
  francuski. Mapuj po prefiksie `2.2`/`3.1`/`3.2`; reszta → domyślny 3.1 + flaga.
- **Zabezpieczenie: 12 wariantów** z literówkami (`NIEOLIWINY`, `NIEOLIWIONY/A/E`, `E-PASYWACJA…`).
  Uwaga: dla HRS kalkulator może w ogóle nie mieć przełącznika oliwienia (jest tylko
  `crZabezp`/`hdgZabezp` dla CR/HDG) — dla HRS ta kolumna jest nie-mapowalna, pomijamy.
- **Zgrzew: 6 wariantów** → `crZgrzew`/`hdgZgrzew`: „…DOZWOLONY Z OZNACZENIEM"→(−3),
  „…DOZWOLONY BEZ OZNACZEN"→(inny/0), „NIEDOZWOLONY"/„Niedozwolony"→(niedozwolony).
  Porównanie case-insensitive, po słowach kluczowych.
- **Płaskość: A/B/C/X/N/FG** + osobna liczbowa tolerancja (nasz model: mały przełącznik,
  tolerancji liczbowej NIE przechowujemy). Mapuj kod→wartość `sscFlatness`, tolerancję pomiń.
- **Powierzchnia: 15 wartości** (HB3/T1/T1I/MSE/…) → `sscSurface`. Mapuj częste, resztę domyślnie.
- **Kształt:** SH/SHT = arkusz. SS/SW/DIV — rzadkie (≈150/15k), **który = krąg? — NIEUSTALONE**,
  do potwierdzenia przez użytkownika. Domyślnie traktuj wszystko poza jawnym kodem kręgu jako arkusz.

## Pola, których plik NIE niesie → wartości domyślne (edytowalne w podglądzie)
Marża % (dom. **7%**), extra (**0**), transport (**0**), `pglBase` (bieżąca baza, dom. 645),
oraz **tonaż = 1 t** (plik nie ma ilości). Dużo pod-przełączników dopłat (crZabezp/crOpak/
crPowierz/crWykon, sscLenTol/sscMarking/sscLabels) też nie są w pliku → domyślne.

## Przeliczanie ceny (recepta z `components/Calculator.tsx`)
```
cenaWsadu   = pglBase + sumaHuta
sumaHuta    = dimSurcharge(grubość,szer) + gradeValue + tolThick + cert + coating + crExtra
sumaSSC     = base + lenTol + flatness + surface + maxWeight + marking + edging + yield + packing + labels + scrap
cenaKoncowa = cenaWsadu + marża% + extra + transport + sumaSSC
```
**Refactor konieczny przed budową:** logika ceny siedzi w `Calculator.tsx` w `useMemo`
(domknięcia po stanie). Wyciągnąć czystą funkcję `computePrice(inputs)` do `lib/`, żeby
import mógł wycenić każdy wiersz niezależnie (i żeby podgląd pokazywał przeliczoną cenę).
Kalkulator potem woła to samo `computePrice`.

## Decyzje UX (już ustalone)
- **Krok podglądu + potwierdzenia**: parsuj → tabela podglądu z przeliczoną ceną i flagami
  dla pól domyślnych/niezmapowanych/wieloznacznych → użytkownik przegląda i edytuje →
  dopiero wtedy pozycje wchodzą do zestawienia. Kluczowe przy tak zaśmieconym pliku.
- **Miejsce importu**: kalkulator (obok przycisku eksportu Excel) **oraz** listy ofert
  (Moje Oferty / Panel Seniora / Admin → Oferty).

## Otwarte pytania przed wznowieniem
1. **Który kod `Kształt` = krąg?** (SS / SW / DIV — czy któryś?) Bez tego import kręgu zgaduje.
2. **Wieloznaczne gatunki** — potwierdzić strategię „auto niższa + flaga" vs blokada wiersza.
3. **Prawdziwe kody do EKSPORTU** — poprawić `lib/excelExport.ts`, żeby emitował realne kody
   grupy (HRBL/CRAS/HDZ…) zamiast surowych HRS/CR/HDG (asymetria round-tripa).
4. **EGZE** (ocynk elektrolityczny) — jak traktować (1 wiersz w 15k, ale istnieje).
5. Zakres słowników best-effort dla Pakowania/Atestu/Zabezpieczenia — ile wariantów mapować
   ręcznie, gdzie próg „→ domyślne + flaga".

## Pliki, których dotknie budowa
- **NOWY** `lib/excelImport.ts` — parser + słowniki odwrotne + mapowanie wiersz→wejścia.
- **NOWY** `lib/computePrice.ts` (refactor) — czysta funkcja ceny wyciągnięta z kalkulatora.
- `components/Calculator.tsx` — przycisk importu + modal podglądu; przejście na `computePrice`.
- Listy ofert (`app/offers`, `app/senior`, `app/admin/oferty`) — przycisk importu.
- `lib/excelExport.ts` — poprawka realnych kodów grupy (punkt 3 wyżej).

# Import z Excela (KTS/GPAO) — analiza formatu i mapowanie

> **STATUS: PRZEANALIZOWANE I ODŁOŻONE (2026-07-08).** Logika mapowania rozpisana
> na podstawie DWÓCH prawdziwych plików eksportu z obecnego systemu. Budowa wstrzymana
> — wracamy do tematu później. Ten dokument jest punktem startowym przy wznowieniu:
> zaczynamy od realnych danych, nie od zera.

## Po co ten dokument
Import to druga (niezrobiona) połowa funkcji eksport/import. Cel: wczytać plik `.xlsx`
w formacie eksportu z obecnego systemu → zmapować kolumny na wejścia kalkulatora →
**przeliczyć cenę** → wstawić pozycje do zestawienia. Główny docelowy use-case: wysyłka
ofert do klientów e-mailem.

Kluczowe odkrycie: **prawdziwy eksport jest DUŻO bardziej zaśmiecony niż model kalkulatora.**
To nie jest czysta odwrotność naszego eksportu — to mapowanie bogatszego, chaotycznego
słownika zewnętrznego na nasze wąskie przełączniki. Wierne odwzorowanie każdej kolumny
jest nierealne; odzyskujemy pewnie tylko rdzeń cenotwórczy, resztę robimy best-effort + flaga.

## Przeanalizowane pliki (prawdziwe eksporty)
1. `exportfile1.xlsx` — arkusz **`KTS`**, 106 wierszy, 43 kolumny (37 „naszych" + 6 pustych
   końcowych). Wyłącznie HRS.
2. `EXPORT_20260522_134555 (1).xlsx` — arkusz **`Data`**, **15 307 wierszy**, 37 kolumn.
   Wszystkie rodziny materiału. To jest reprezentatywny, produkcyjny eksport.

**Wniosek dot. formatu:** nazwa arkusza NIE jest stała (`KTS` vs `Data`) — import musi
znaleźć arkusz po dopasowaniu nagłówków, nie po nazwie. Liczba kolumn też się waha
(43 vs 37) — bierzemy pierwsze 37 wg `KTS_HEADERS` z `lib/excelExport.ts`, resztę ignorujemy.

## Mapowania — co odzyskujemy PEWNIE (rdzeń cenotwórczy)

### Grupa materiałowa → typ stali
| Kod w pliku | Rodzina | → nasz typ |
|---|---|---|
| HRBL, HRB, HRPI | gorącowalcowana (czarna / — / trawiona) | **HRS** |
| CRAS | zimnowalcowana | **CR** |
| HDZ, HDZM | ocynk ogniowy | **HDG** |
| EGZE | ocynk elektrolityczny (1 wiersz w 15k — pomijalne) | (edge-case, do decyzji) |
| *(puste)* | brak grupy (356 wierszy) | flaga w podglądzie |

> Uwaga o asymetrii round-tripa: nasz **eksport** zapisuje surowe `HRS`/`CR`/`HDG`, które
> NIE pasują do żadnego realnego kodu (`HRBL` itd.). Przy okazji importu trzeba poprawić
> też eksport, żeby emitował prawdziwe kody — inaczej nasz-eksport→nasz-import i
> prawdziwy-eksport→nasz-import to dwa różne słowniki.

### Gatunek → wartość dopłaty (NAJWAŻNIEJSZE — steruje ceną)
Normalizacja: `UPPER`, usuń `®`, zwiń spacje, `.`→`_` (albo oba na nic), usuń `(NN)`.
Na pliku 1 (17 gatunków): **13/17 trafia jednoznacznie**, 2 wieloznaczne, 2 bez trafienia.
- **Wieloznaczne** (ta sama nazwa = dwie różne dopłaty w naszej tabeli):
  `S355MC` → 48 albo 68; `S355J2C+N-CAT.A` → 57 albo 72.
  Obsługa: auto-wybór (domyślnie niższa) + **podświetlenie wiersza w podglądzie** do ręcznej
  korekty. (Decyzja do potwierdzenia — patrz „Otwarte pytania".)
- **Bez trafienia** (za bardzo inna pisownia): `AMStrongUlt700MC`, `AMStrongUlt700MCT`
  → u nas `Amstrong® Ultra 700MC_B` / `Amstrong® Ultra 700MCT` (obie =165).
  Obsługa: **mała ręczna mapa aliasów** na górze parsera.
- Reszta bez trafienia → flaga „nierozpoznany gatunek" + ręczny wybór w podglądzie.

### Wymiary
`Grubość` / `Szerokość` / `Długość` — czyste liczby. `dimSurcharge` liczymy z grubości+szer.
przez istniejącą `getDimensionSurcharge`. Bez problemu.

### Pokrycie (tylko HDG) → `selectedCoating`
Odzyskiwalne, wymaga normalizacji: `275`≡`Z275`, `+Z275`≡`Z275`; są też `Z100/Z180/Z225`,
`ZM120/ZM175/ZM250/ZM310`, `+ZM430`, `+DBL 25/25`. Zbudować mapę „surowe → kod powłoki".

## Mapowania best-effort (zaśmiecone kolumny — mapuj częste, resztę domyślnie + flaga)
Realny plik ma znacznie więcej wariancji niż nasze przełączniki:
- **Pakowanie: 72 różne wartości** (my mamy 6: S01/S03/S12/S13/SB2/SB3). Wolny tekst, literówki,
  zepsute kodowanie (`kant�wkach`), francuski, opisy typu „2 X BELKI POPRZ. DLG. 1000".
  Mapuj tylko czyste kody S01/S03/… → indeks przełącznika; reszta → domyślny S01 + flaga.
- **Atest: 21 wariantów** (my: 3 → 2.2/3.1/3.2). `+CE`, `+AD2000W1`, `Without`, `BEZ ATESTU`,
  francuski. Mapuj po prefiksie `2.2`/`3.1`/`3.2`; reszta → domyślny 3.1 + flaga.
- **Zabezpieczenie: 12 wariantów** z literówkami (`NIEOLIWINY`, `NIEOLIWIONY/A/E`, `E-PASYWACJA…`).
  Uwaga: dla HRS kalkulator może w ogóle nie mieć przełącznika oliwienia (jest tylko
  `crZabezp`/`hdgZabezp` dla CR/HDG) — dla HRS ta kolumna jest nie-mapowalna, pomijamy.
- **Zgrzew: 6 wariantów** → `crZgrzew`/`hdgZgrzew`: „…DOZWOLONY Z OZNACZENIEM"→(−3),
  „…DOZWOLONY BEZ OZNACZEN"→(inny/0), „NIEDOZWOLONY"/„Niedozwolony"→(niedozwolony).
  Porównanie case-insensitive, po słowach kluczowych.
- **Płaskość: A/B/C/X/N/FG** + osobna liczbowa tolerancja (nasz model: mały przełącznik,
  tolerancji liczbowej NIE przechowujemy). Mapuj kod→wartość `sscFlatness`, tolerancję pomiń.
- **Powierzchnia: 15 wartości** (HB3/T1/T1I/MSE/…) → `sscSurface`. Mapuj częste, resztę domyślnie.
- **Kształt:** SH/SHT = arkusz. SS/SW/DIV — rzadkie (≈150/15k), **który = krąg? — NIEUSTALONE**,
  do potwierdzenia przez użytkownika. Domyślnie traktuj wszystko poza jawnym kodem kręgu jako arkusz.

## Pola, których plik NIE niesie → wartości domyślne (edytowalne w podglądzie)
Marża % (dom. **7%**), extra (**0**), transport (**0**), `pglBase` (bieżąca baza, dom. 645),
oraz **tonaż = 1 t** (plik nie ma ilości). Dużo pod-przełączników dopłat (crZabezp/crOpak/
crPowierz/crWykon, sscLenTol/sscMarking/sscLabels) też nie są w pliku → domyślne.

## Przeliczanie ceny (recepta z `components/Calculator.tsx`)
```
cenaWsadu   = pglBase + sumaHuta
sumaHuta    = dimSurcharge(grubość,szer) + gradeValue + tolThick + cert + coating + crExtra
sumaSSC     = base + lenTol + flatness + surface + maxWeight + marking + edging + yield + packing + labels + scrap
cenaKoncowa = cenaWsadu + marża% + extra + transport + sumaSSC
```
**Refactor konieczny przed budową:** logika ceny siedzi w `Calculator.tsx` w `useMemo`
(domknięcia po stanie). Wyciągnąć czystą funkcję `computePrice(inputs)` do `lib/`, żeby
import mógł wycenić każdy wiersz niezależnie (i żeby podgląd pokazywał przeliczoną cenę).
Kalkulator potem woła to samo `computePrice`.

## Decyzje UX (już ustalone)
- **Krok podglądu + potwierdzenia**: parsuj → tabela podglądu z przeliczoną ceną i flagami
  dla pól domyślnych/niezmapowanych/wieloznacznych → użytkownik przegląda i edytuje →
  dopiero wtedy pozycje wchodzą do zestawienia. Kluczowe przy tak zaśmieconym pliku.
- **Miejsce importu**: kalkulator (obok przycisku eksportu Excel) **oraz** listy ofert
  (Moje Oferty / Panel Seniora / Admin → Oferty).

## Otwarte pytania przed wznowieniem
1. **Który kod `Kształt` = krąg?** (SS / SW / DIV — czy któryś?) Bez tego import kręgu zgaduje.
2. **Wieloznaczne gatunki** — potwierdzić strategię „auto niższa + flaga" vs blokada wiersza.
3. **Prawdziwe kody do EKSPORTU** — poprawić `lib/excelExport.ts`, żeby emitował realne kody
   grupy (HRBL/CRAS/HDZ…) zamiast surowych HRS/CR/HDG (asymetria round-tripa).
4. **EGZE** (ocynk elektrolityczny) — jak traktować (1 wiersz w 15k, ale istnieje).
5. Zakres słowników best-effort dla Pakowania/Atestu/Zabezpieczenia — ile wariantów mapować
   ręcznie, gdzie próg „→ domyślne + flaga".

## Pliki, których dotknie budowa
- **NOWY** `lib/excelImport.ts` — parser + słowniki odwrotne + mapowanie wiersz→wejścia.
- **NOWY** `lib/computePrice.ts` (refactor) — czysta funkcja ceny wyciągnięta z kalkulatora.
- `components/Calculator.tsx` — przycisk importu + modal podglądu; przejście na `computePrice`.
- Listy ofert (`app/offers`, `app/senior`, `app/admin/oferty`) — przycisk importu.
- `lib/excelExport.ts` — poprawka realnych kodów grupy (punkt 3 wyżej).

Usage: claude-flow hooks <subcommand> [options]

Subcommands:
  - pre-edit        - Get context before editing files
  - post-edit       - Record editing outcomes for learning

  - post-command    - Record command execution outcomes

  - post-task       - Record task completion for learning

  - session-restore - Restore a previous session
  - route           - Route tasks to optimal agents
  - explain         - Explain routing decisions
  - pretrain        - Bootstrap intelligence from repository
  - build-agents    - Generate optimized agent configs

  - transfer        - Transfer patterns from another project

`tsc --noEmit` passes clean (exit 0) — which is the real proof here: because `cs` and `de` are typed as `Translations` and the map is `Record<Language, Translations>`, the compiler verified **all 312 keys are present in both languages** with correct types. No missing keys, no typos in structure.

## Done — Czech 🇨🇿 and German 🇩🇪 added

**`lib/translations.ts`**
- `Language` type → `'pl' | 'en' | 'cs' | 'de'`
- Full `cs` and `de` translation objects (all 312 keys), registered in the `translations` map
- Steel-industry terms handled properly, not literal: e.g. *Mill surcharges* → CS `Hutní příplatky` / DE `Hüttenzuschläge`, *Flatness* → `Rovinnost` / `Ebenheit`, *Yield strength* → `Mez kluzu` / `Streckgrenze`, *Grade* → `Jakost` / `Güte`, *Besäumen* for edging, etc.

**`contexts/LanguageContext.tsx`**
- localStorage guard now accepts `cs`/`de` (so the choice persists across reloads)
- Added `CzechFlag` and `GermanFlag` SVGs; `LanguageFlag` and `LanguageSelector` now render all four via a small map/loop instead of a pl/en ternary

- `toggleLanguage()` (the old pl↔en toggle) I left as-is — nothing uses it in the UI (the selector calls `setLanguage` directly), so it's harmless, but it only flips pl/en. Easy to make it cycle all four later if anything ever calls it.
- Translations are solid conversational Czech/German, but for **customer-facing PDF** wording you may want a native speaker to eyeball the `pdf.*` section (terms/validity/payment phrasing) before sending real quotes abroad.

content.text:
Server's healthy — home returns 200, Next.js hot-reloaded cleanly (`✓ Compiled`, no errors). 

## Offer sorting added — done for today 🎯

**On the "Moje Oferty" page** (`app/offers/page.tsx`):
- Sort control appears in the list header (only when there's more than 1 offer): a **dropdown** (Date / Name / Value / Status) + a **▲/▼ direction toggle**
- **Default: newest first** (Date, descending) — matches what you'd expect opening the list
- Sort keys:
  - **Date** → by `created_at`
  - **Name** → locale-aware, case-insensitive
  - **Value** → by the offer's total (sum of `totalValue`)
  - **Status** → by workflow order (draft → pending → approved → rejected → sent)
- Ties break by creation date so the order is stable
- Sorts a **copy** via `useMemo` — never mutates state; re-sorts only when offers/key/direction change

**Fully localized** — added a `sort` section to the `Translations` interface and all four languages (PL/EN/CS/DE), so the new controls read correctly whichever flag is active.

Two honest notes:
- I did **only the My Offers page**, as scoped. The **Senior** and **Admin → Oferty** lists have their own separate rendering and don't have sorting yet — easy to replicate the same pattern there next time.
- This is client-side sorting of whatever the API returns (fine for normal offer counts). If the list ever grows huge, sorting would want to move server-side — not a concern now.

Everything's **local and uncommitted**, as you asked. The CS/DE translations + the sorting are all sitting in your working tree ready whenever you want to commit. Have a good rest of your day.

# UI UX Pro Max Skill Repository

## Purpose
This is an AI skill providing design intelligence for building professional UI/UX across multiple platforms and frameworks. The v2.0 flagship feature is an "Intelligent Design System Generator" that analyzes project requirements and generates tailored design systems using a reasoning engine.

Yes. The repository contains skill configuration files (`.claude-plugin/` directory) and supports Claude Code installation.

```
.claude-plugin/          # Plugin configuration

cli/                     # CLI installer (generates platform files)
docs/                    # Documentation
preview/                 # Preview files
projects/                # Project templates
screenshots/             # Images
scripts/                 # Utility scripts

skill.json              # Skill metadata
README.md               # Main documentation
CLAUDE.md               # Development guidelines
CONTRIBUTING.md         # Contribution guide
LICENSE                 # MIT license
```

**Marketplace method:**
```
/plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill
```

**CLI method (recommended):**

```
npm install -g ui-ux-pro-max-cli
cd /path/to/your/project
uipro init --ai claude      # Claude Code
uipro init --ai cursor      # Cursor
uipro init --ai windsurf    # Windsurf
```

# shadcn MCP Server Setup for Claude Code

## Quick Setup Command

Run this in your project:
```bash
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude
```

## Manual Configuration

Add this to your `.mcp.json` file:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shadcn": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["shadcn@latest", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Then restart Claude Code and run `/mcp` to verify connection.

## API Key Requirements

**No API key is required** for the standard shadcn/ui registry. However, if you're using private registries, you'll need to configure authentication by setting environment variables in `.env.local`:

```
REGISTRY_TOKEN=your_token_here
API_KEY=your_api_key_here
```

These credentials are only needed when accessing registries that require authentication, which you specify in your `components.json` file using custom registry URLs with authorization headers.

|---|---|---|

Two honest notes before I run anything:

1. **`frontend-design` is already installed** — it's in my active skill list right now (`frontend-design:frontend-design`). So you don't need the anthropics/skills repo *for that one*. What that marketplace actually adds is **`document-skills`** (PDF / docx / xlsx / pptx manipulation) and `example-skills` — and the **xlsx + PDF ones are genuinely relevant** to your SteelQuote Excel/PDF export work. That's the real reason to add it, not frontend-design.

2. **Curation reality check** — you're now stacking a *lot* of overlapping design skills: the 7-skill ui-ux-pro-max family, frontend-design, plus taste (design taste), motion-principles (animation), impeccable (design quality). They're lazy-loaded so it's not harmful, but past a point they blur into each other and it's not obvious which fires. My honest suggestion: these three — **taste, motion, impeccable** — are the most differentiated (taste = aesthetic judgment, motion = animation specifically, impeccable = polish audit), so they add real range. Now I can see the difference clearly:

- **design-motion-principles** = 1 clean, well-scoped skill (motion/animation audit). Easy yes.
- **taste-skill** = **13 skills**, and most are **image-generation** (`brandkit`, `imagegen-frontend-web`, `imagegen-frontend-mobile`, `image-to-code`…) — those generate design *images*, not code, and lean on image-gen backends. Only a few are coding/taste skills (`gpt-taste`, `minimalist-ui`, `industrial-brutalist-ui`). Installing all 13 would flood your skill list with image-gen tools you may not want.

Let me install the clean one now and pull the full taste-skill list so we can cherry-pick:

# fallback: just grab the cyan skill names

# ECC: Agent Harness Operating System

## What It Is

ECC (the acronym is not explicitly defined in the README) is a comprehensive system for optimizing AI agent harnesses. The project describes itself as "The harness-native operator system for agentic work. Built from real-world multi-harness engineering workflows."

## Problem & Solution

ECC solves the challenge of coordinating work across multiple AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Codex, etc.). Rather than requiring separate configurations for each tool, it provides a unified system that works cross-platform with shared components.

## Main Features

- **67 agents** for delegated task handling
- **277+ skills** providing reusable workflows
- **Hook system** for event-triggered automations
- **Rules framework** organizing best practices by language
- **Memory persistence** across sessions
- **Continuous learning** via instinct extraction
- **Security scanning** through AgentShield integration
- **MCP configurations** for external tool integration

## Architecture

ECC is primarily a **Claude Code plugin** with manual installation fallbacks. The tech stack includes:

- Shell scripts (Bash/PowerShell)
- Node.js/TypeScript
- Python
- YAML/Markdown for configuration

Components include agents, skills, commands, hooks, and rules organized in a modular directory structure.

## Key Claims

The README emphasizes "production-ready" status, "10+ months of intensive daily use," and support for "12+ language ecosystems." It positions itself as "not just configs" but a complete system including optimization, security, and research-first development patterns.

## Installation

**Plugin path (recommended):**
```
/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC
/plugin install ecc@ecc
```

**Manual installation:**
```
git clone https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC.git
cd ECC
npm install
./install.sh --profile full
```

The README emphasizes not stacking install methods and warns against duplicating plugin installs.

Now I can compare them properly. They're actually **different species** of tool, which matters for your decision.

## What each one is

| | **ruflo** (installed) | **ECC** |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Live **MCP-server swarm** — hundreds of runtime tools | **Plugin bundle** — agents + skills + hooks + rules |
| **Core idea** | Autonomous multi-agent orchestration: `swarm_init`, `hive-mind`, `agent_spawn`, shared `agentdb` memory, `neural_train`, consensus | "Harness operating system": 67 curated agents, 277+ skills, per-language rules, hooks, memory, AgentShield security scan |
| **Lineage** | claude-flow ecosystem (ruvnet) — sprawling, ambitious | One engineer's (affaan-m) refined daily-use kit, cross-harness (Claude/Cursor/Codex) |
| **Weight** | Very heavy — that giant deferred-tool list *is* ruflo | Heavy too, but skill/agent-based (lazy-loaded, less tool-namespace bloat) |
| **Install** | already active (MCP + `ruflo-core` plugin) | `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` → `/plugin install ecc@ecc` |

## The honest read for *your* use

Your actual work with me is practical Next.js/Postgres feature shipping — read code, edit, typecheck, run the dev server, ship. **Neither is needed for that.** We haven't touched a single ruflo tool this entire session; it's been inert background noise (those `[INTELLIGENCE]` reminders, the enormous tool list — all ruflo).

- **ruflo** = the "team of autonomous agents / neural swarm" fantasy. Genuinely overkill for a solo dev on one app, and it's the biggest *noise* source in your setup — huge tool namespace, auto-injected CLAUDE.md, speculative stuff (WASM agents, metaharness, ruvllm) you'll likely never run.
- **ECC** = closer to practical daily coding: language rules, hooks, security scanning, curated agents, and it's cross-harness if you also use Cursor/Codex. More useful *shape* for real work — **but** 277 skills + 67 agents would bury the design skills you just hand-picked (ui-ux-pro-max, taste cluster, impeccable, document-skills), and its hooks/rules change harness behavior in ways you'd want to understand first.

## My recommendation
Don't run both — that's two overlapping meta-frameworks fighting for the same space. Concretely:

1. **If you want lean + practical:** you don't need a swarm at all. I'd actually **trim ruflo** (most noise, least use for you), and if you want a curated agent/rules/hooks layer, install **ECC but *not* `--profile full`** — pick a minimal profile so it doesn't drown your curated skills.
2. **If you're in "collect and experiment" mode:** ECC is the better-aligned of the two for coding; ruflo is the flashier "multi-agent" idea but the heavier, noisier one.

Two caveats: both are third-party with full tool permissions (same "review before trusting" note as the skills), and I can't fully judge ECC's runtime hooks/rules without installing it.

Want me to (a) show you how to trim ruflo down, (b) install ECC on a minimal profile so we can look at it, or (c) leave it and just get you Remotion before you log off?

So any setup has to serve *both* lanes: shipping app features **and** wrangling Python/ML/Docker/automation. Here's my honest opinion.

## First — the thing you're most worried about is already solved
You said you want to type "make me good frontend colours, bla bla" and have me just *use the right tools* — no `/commands`. **That already works.** Skills auto-fire on their descriptions. If you say *"give SteelQuote a nicer palette,"* I automatically reach for `design-taste-frontend` / `ui-ux-pro-max` (it has 161 palettes) / `dataviz` — you type nothing special. Slash commands are only for a handful of meta-actions (`/plugin`, `/code-review`). **Your natural-language → right-tool workflow is the default, not something you need to build.**

## Second — your instinct is right: you have too much, not too little
More skills ≠ better. The real problem in your current setup is **overlap**. You now have *four* things that all answer "make this UI good": `ui-ux-pro-max` (8 skills), the taste cluster (5), `impeccable`, and `frontend-design`. When they all match a prompt, it's ambiguous which fires, and they dilute each other. **Curation beats accumulation.** A tight set I reliably reach for is worth more than a sprawling library.

## My opinionated solo-founder stack

**Keep (high value, both lanes):**
- **One design lane, not four.** I'd keep **`impeccable`** *or* **`ui-ux-pro-max`** as the primary, plus **`design-motion-principles`** for animation. Drop the rest to background.
- **`document-skills`** (xlsx/pdf/docx/pptx) — real for a founder: client exports, pitch decks, reports. You literally do Excel/PDF in SteelQuote.
- **`shadcn` MCP** — component work, concrete.
- **`context7` MCP** (you have it pending) — pulls *current* library docs. For a solo dev jumping across Next.js/FastAPI/Celery/ComfyUI, this is genuinely high-leverage.
- **`playwright` MCP** (also pending) — browser automation + UI verification. Bonus: directly relevant to synthara's social automation.

**Cut (noise for you):**
- **ruflo's swarm/hive-mind/neural/WASM/metaharness.** You don't use swarms, they need a different subscription, and they're the single biggest source of noise (that gigantic tool list, the auto-injected CLAUDE.md, the `[INTELLIGENCE]` reminders). **Situational (turn on per need):** GitHub MCP (if you live in PRs), Supabase MCP (if that's your DB), Notion (if you plan there).

Not a tool — it's **context**. The most reliable way to make me "Luna who just gets it" is a sharp **CLAUDE.md** (global + per-project) plus memory, encoding: your stack, your taste ("dark, editorial, no generic AI gradients"), and rules like *"for UI always use impeccable; for exports use document-skills."* That steers me far more consistently than stacking overlapping skills. You've already got the auto-memory going — that's the right foundation.

For *you* specifically: **neither swarm framework is the win.** ruflo is mostly dead weight for a solo dev without the swarm subscription. ECC is better-shaped for real coding, but full-install would bury your curated skills under 277 more. If you ever try ECC, minimal profile only. That's lean, serves both SteelQuote and synthara, and keeps the "I talk, Luna does the right thing" flow you actually want.

Think it over — when you're ready I can help you trim ruflo, pick the design lane, and write a tight global CLAUDE.md. Nothing installed or changed yet, as you asked.
